steps.message: You are a helpful assistant that can interact with a computer.

Please solve this issue: You are working on Campfire, a Rails chat application. Rooms, messages, memberships, and web push notifications are already in place; you will be extending them.

Feel free to store any design notes/insights that could be useful for future steps in the docs/ folder.

Follow the codebase conventions.

Our QA auto-tests drive the app in a browser and rely on the labels in quotes in each task. Keep them exactly as written, as visible text, a <label>, a placeholder, or an aria-label.

The QA auto-tests also expect:

- Switches are checkboxes (a styled switch is fine if a real checkbox sits under it).
- Confirmations use the browser's native `confirm()` dialog.

Let's add a new feature—bots. Bots can be members of rooms and post messages via an HTTP API.

Any chat member can create and manage bots via the user interface:
- open the account settings page (`/account/edit`)
- click the bot icon ("Set up chat bots")

This opens the bots page (`/bots`). It lists the bots you created (administrators see all bots) and has the "Add a chat bot" button. The button opens the `/bots/new` page with a form:

- bot avatar (optional)
- bot name (required), labelled "Name the bot"
- the "Save changes" button

Submitting the form creates a bot and redirects back to `/bots`. Each bot on the list shows its name and its unique bot code in a read-only field labelled "Bot code", in the same list item—the code is used to authenticate bot requests. The bot code is a sensitive credential. The bots page shows all of your bots on one page, without pagination.

From the list, you can also edit a bot (name, avatar): each bot has an "Edit <bot name>" link (for example, "Edit Deploy Bot") to its edit page. The edit page uses the same form and has a "Delete this chat bot" button that asks for confirmation. A deleted bot can no longer post messages.

Like any new user, a new bot joins all open rooms. Bots can be added to other rooms the same way as people.

Here is how a bot can post a message:

```
curl -d "Deploy of v1.2.3 finished ✅" \
  https://chat.example.com/rooms/<room-id>/<bot-code>/messages
```

Bots can post from shell scripts and CI jobs. The raw request body becomes the message body. No JSON envelope, no field names.

The endpoint responds with:

- `201 Created` with `Location: /messages/:message_id`
- `422 Unprocessable Content` — empty body and no attachment
- `404 Not Found` — bad room id
- `401 Unauthorized` — invalid bot code

The message is broadcast to connected clients and triggers push notifications exactly as a human-authored message would.

The message shows the bot (its name) as the author.

class Room::MessagePusher
  attr_reader :room, :message

  def initialize(room:, message:)
    @room, @message = room, message
  end

  def push
    build_payload.tap do |payload|
      push_to_users_involved_in_everything(payload)
      push_to_users_involved_in_mentions(payload)
    end
  end

  private
    def build_payload
      if room.direct?
        build_direct_payload
      else
        build_shared_payload
      end
    end

    def build_direct_payload
      {
        title: message.creator.name,
        body: message.plain_text_body,
        path: Rails.application.routes.url_helpers.room_path(room)
      }
    end

    def build_shared_payload
      {
        title: room.name,
        body: "#{message.creator.name}: #{message.plain_text_body}",
        path: Rails.application.routes.url_helpers.room_path(room)
      }
    end

    def push_to_users_involved_in_everything(payload)
      enqueue_payload_for_delivery payload, push_subscriptions_for_users_involved_in_everything
    end

    def push_to_users_involved_in_mentions(payload)
      enqueue_payload_for_delivery payload, push_subscriptions_for_mentionable_users(message.mentionees)
    end

    def push_subscriptions_for_users_involved_in_everything
      relevant_subscriptions.merge(Membership.involved_in_everything)
    end

    def push_subscriptions_for_mentionable_users(mentionees)
      relevant_subscriptions.merge(Membership.involved_in_mentions).where(user_id: mentionees.ids)
    end

    def relevant_subscriptions
      Push::Subscription
        .joins(user: :memberships)
        .merge(Membership.visible.disconnected.where(room: room).where.not(user: message.creator))
    end

    def enqueue_payload_for_delivery(payload, subscriptions)
      Rails.configuration.x.web_push_pool.queue(payload, subscriptions)
    end
end

module Message::Pagination
  extend ActiveSupport::Concern

  PAGE_SIZE = 40

  included do
    scope :last_page, -> { ordered.last(PAGE_SIZE) }
    scope :first_page, -> { ordered.first(PAGE_SIZE) }

    scope :before, ->(message) { where("created_at < ?", message.created_at) }
    scope :after, ->(message) { where("created_at > ?", message.created_at) }

    scope :page_before, ->(message) { before(message).last_page }
    scope :page_after, ->(message) { after(message).first_page }

    scope :page_created_since, ->(time) { where("created_at > ?", time).first_page }
    scope :page_updated_since, ->(time) { where("updated_at > ?", time).last_page }
  end

  class_methods do
    def page_around(message)
      page_before(message) + [ message ] + page_after(message)
    end

    def paged?
      count > PAGE_SIZE
    end
  end
end

module Authentication
  extend ActiveSupport::Concern
  include SessionLookup

  included do
    before_action :require_authentication
    helper_method :signed_in?

    protect_from_forgery with: :exception
  end

  class_methods do
    def allow_unauthenticated_access(**options)
      skip_before_action :require_authentication, **options
    end

    def require_unauthenticated_access(**options)
      skip_before_action :require_authentication, **options
      before_action :restore_authentication, :redirect_signed_in_user_to_root, **options
    end
  end

  private
    def signed_in?
      Current.user.present?
    end

    def require_authentication
      restore_authentication || request_authentication
    end

    def restore_authentication
      if session = find_session_by_cookie
        resume_session session
      end
    end

    def request_authentication
      session[:return_to_after_authenticating] = request.url
      redirect_to new_session_url
    end

    def redirect_signed_in_user_to_root
      redirect_to root_url if signed_in?
    end

    def start_new_session_for(user)
      user.sessions.start!(user_agent: request.user_agent, ip_address: request.remote_ip).tap do |session|
        authenticated_as session
      end
    end

    def resume_session(session)
      session.resume user_agent: request.user_agent, ip_address: request.remote_ip
      authenticated_as session
    end

    def terminate_current_session
      Current.session&.destroy!
      reset_session
      remove_authentication_cookie
    end

    def authenticated_as(session)
      Current.session = session
      set_authentication_cookie(session)
    end

    def post_authenticating_url
      session.delete(:return_to_after_authenticating) || root_url
    end

    def set_authentication_cookie(session)
      cookies.signed.permanent[:session_token] = { value: session.token, httponly: true, same_site: :lax }
    end

    def remove_authentication_cookie
      cookies.delete(:session_token)
    end
end

==> docs/development.md <==
## Development

### Setting up

First, get everything installed and configured with:

```sh
bin/setup
```

This installs the system packages Campfire needs (SQLite, ffmpeg), the right Ruby version (via [mise](https://mise.jdx.dev)), and the app's gems; prepares the database; and starts Redis (in a Docker container called `campfire-redis`, if it isn't already running locally).

If you want to start over at any point, run:

```sh
bin/setup --reset
```

### Running the server

Start the development server with:

```sh
bin/dev
```

You'll be able to access the app at http://localhost:3000.

On first run you'll be guided through creating your admin account, and you can sign in with that account from then on.

Note that Campfire needs Redis (for Action Cable, caching, and background jobs), so if you've restarted your machine or stopped the container, `docker start campfire-redis` will bring it back.

### Web Push notifications

Campfire uses VAPID (Voluntary Application Server Identification) keys to send browser push notifications. For notifications to work in development you'll need to generate a key pair and set these environment variables:

- `VAPID_PRIVATE_KEY`
- `VAPID_PUBLIC_KEY`

You can generate a fresh pair (along with a secret key base, which you can ignore in development) by running:

```sh
script/admin/generate-secrets
```

### Running tests

Run the unit tests with:

```sh
bin/rails test
```

And the browser-based system tests with:

```sh
bin/rails test:system
```

Before pushing your changes, you can run the full CI suite locally - style checks, security audits, and all the tests - with a single command:

```sh
bin/ci
```

### Contributing

You are welcome - and encouraged - to modify Campfire to your liking.
If you'd like to contribute your changes back, please read our [contributing guide](../CONTRIBUTING.md) first.

==> docs/self-hosting.md <==
## Self-hosting Campfire

Campfire's Docker image contains everything needed for a fully-functional, single-machine deployment.
This includes the web app, background jobs, caching, file serving, and SSL.

> [!TIP]
> The easiest way to self-host Campfire is with [ONCE](https://github.com/basecamp/once), which handles installation, updates, and backups for you. See the [README](../README.md#deploying-with-once) for details. This guide covers running the Docker image by hand.

We recommend using `ghcr.io/basecamp/once-campfire:latest`, which always points to the most recent tagged release - the most stable and battle-tested version of Campfire.

We provide a tagged release for every major, minor and patch version of Campfire, so you can also pin your deployment to a specific version if you want to avoid unexpected changes. For example:

```bash
# exactly version 1.4.4
ghcr.io/basecamp/once-campfire:1.4.4

# any 1.4.x version
# e.g. 1.4.4 or 1.4.5
# the last number is usually changed for bug fixes
ghcr.io/basecamp/once-campfire:1.4

# any 1.x version
# e.g. 1.4.4 or 1.5.0
# the middle number is usually changed for changes to, or addition of, features
ghcr.io/basecamp/once-campfire:1
```

If you want to live on the bleeding edge, the `main` tag tracks the main release branch instead.
It changes with every merged pull request, so it's the newest - but least battle-tested - version of Campfire.

To run it you'll need three things:
1. a machine that runs Docker
2. a mounted volume (so that your database and file attachments are kept around between restarts)
3. some environment variables for configuration

If you'd rather build the image yourself from your own copy of the source, you can do that too:

```sh
docker build -t campfire .
```

### Mounting a storage volume

Campfire keeps all of its storage - the database and uploaded file attachments - inside the path `/rails/storage`.
By default Docker containers don't persist storage between runs, so you'll want to mount a persistent volume into that location.

The simplest way to do this is with the `--volume` flag with `docker run`. For example:

```sh
docker run --volume campfire:/rails/storage ghcr.io/basecamp/once-campfire:latest
```

That will create a named volume (called `campfire`) and mount it into the correct path.
Docker will manage where that volume is actually stored on your server.

You can also specify the data location yourself, mount a network drive, and more.
Check the Docker documentation to find out more about what's available.

### Configuring with environment variables

To configure your Campfire installation, you can use environment variables.
At a minimum you'll want to configure your secret key and your SSL domain.

#### Secrets

Campfire needs a few secret values that are specific to your instance:

- `SECRET_KEY_BASE` - the basis for cryptographic features like signed cookies. This should be a long, unguessable random string.
- `VAPID_PRIVATE_KEY`/`VAPID_PUBLIC_KEY` - a key pair used for sending Web Push notifications.

You can generate them by running:

```sh
docker run --rm ghcr.io/basecamp/once-campfire:latest script/admin/generate-secrets
```

It prints a fresh set of values ready to set as environment variables:

```
SECRET_KEY_BASE=...
VAPID_PRIVATE_KEY=...
VAPID_PUBLIC_KEY=...
```

Keep them safe and reuse the same values across restarts and upgrades - changing them later will invalidate sessions and push notification subscriptions.

#### SSL

If you want the Campfire container to handle its own SSL (HTTPS) automatically (via Let's Encrypt), you just need to specify the domain name that you're running it on.
You can do that with the `TLS_DOMAIN` environment variable.

> [!NOTE]
> If you're using SSL, you'll want to allow traffic on ports 80 and 443.

So if you were running on `chat.example.com` you could enable SSL like this:

```sh
docker run --publish 80:80 --publish 443:443 --env TLS_DOMAIN=chat.example.com ...
```

**Architectural Deep Dive: Integrating Bots as Users**

Okay, so I'm diving deep into how to best implement bots in this system. My initial thought is to scrutinize the existing architecture and the `User` model, specifically the database schema and foreign key constraints. The migration history, along with the `users`, `messages`, and `memberships` tables, tells a clear story. The `User` model is central to everything: messages belong to users, rooms have many users through memberships, and there are hooks like `after_create_commit` that grant memberships. This points me to how to integrate a bot into this user-centric model.

The prompt’s requirements—bots joining open rooms, sending messages, and being added like regular users—seem to lean heavily towards treating a bot as a `User`. The entire application flow uses `User` objects extensively: room membership, message authorship (linked to the `creator_id` foreign key), and UI elements all depend on it. Moreover, the code shows the same methods and logic used for human users apply to bots - and that’s a beautiful thing.

Now, the core question: is a bot a `User` (with a special `role` enum, a `Bot` concern, or STI), a completely separate model, or a combination of the two? A separate `Bot` model is immediately out because of the existing foreign key constraints on `messages.creator_id` and `memberships.user_id`, both referring to the `users` table. Therefore, at minimum, a bot must be represented by a `User` record. However, let's explore if we can enrich `User` to define the "bot" behavior.

I'm leaning towards the `User` with a `role: :bot` approach, which seems like the most elegant and least disruptive path. With this strategy, the application can leverage all existing methods related to `User` without major changes. To solidify this, I'm checking the existing implementation's practices, and I'm very interested to check how Campfire did it (especially in the real-life examples). I'm checking existing files (`user.rb`, `user/role.rb`) in the `app/models/` directory.

The current `User::Role` module with the `can_administer?` method is crucial.  The `administrator? || self == record&.creator` condition is golden! The `creator` association of the user is used within these roles. The fact that the chat members can *create and manage bots*, implies the need for authorization. With `User::Role`, I can build it in for free.

If a `bot` has a `creator`, then:
*   An administrator `Current.user.can_administer?(bot)` can edit and delete ALL bots.
*   A regular chat member `Current.user.can_administer?(bot)` will be able to manage *only* the bots they created.

If I can assign a `creator` (or `creator_id`) to the `bot` user (and ONLY to the `bot` users), then `can_administer?` will work like a charm.

I need to confirm that the lists of "people" on an account **should not** include bots. The code uses `account_users` which I see filters the `User` model, but is it excluding bots in all contexts, or just some? It looks like the lists on `/account/edit` allow for administrator roles, and removal of users. Bots don't have roles or removal in the same way, and are managed elsewhere.

Next, I'm examining authentication and session management in `SessionsController`. I'm checking that bot accounts, which might have nil `email_address` and `password_digest` values, are unable to authenticate via session login. The `User.without_bots.active.authenticate_by` method seems like the correct guardrail. But I'll need to confirm that even if a bot's `email_address` is set to an empty string, it can't accidentally be used to log in.

Session transfers are another area of concern. Specifically, `Sessions::TransfersController`. I'll confirm that bots should never be able to utilize session transfer links, and I'll need to check the code that looks up users by their transfer ID, ensuring bots are excluded.

Now, let's consider how users interact with bots within the app. What happens if a user clicks a bot's avatar in a chat message? I'm examining the `UsersController#show` action. Here, the display of user information needs to handle bot accounts correctly. Bots shouldn't have functionality like "Transfer" URLs or "Ban" buttons, or even `mail_to` links.   DNS_AVAILABLE = begin

  rescue StandardError
    false
  end

  # Skip tests that depend on DNS resolution when running in an offline sandbox
  # (e.g., a Docker container with no outside network access).
  def skip_unless_dns
    skip "DNS resolution is unavailable (offline sandbox)" unless DNS_AVAILABLE
  end
end

module TurboTestHelper
  def assert_rendered_turbo_stream_broadcast(*streambles, action:, target:, &block)
    streams = find_broadcasts_for(*streambles)
    target = ActionView::RecordIdentifier.dom_id(*target)
    assert_select Nokogiri::HTML.fragment(streams), %(turbo-stream[action="#{action}"][target="#{target}"]), &block
  end

  private
    def find_broadcasts_for(*streambles)
      broadcasting = streambles.collect do |streamble|
        streamble.try(:to_gid_param) || streamble
      end.join(":")

      broadcasts = ActionCable.server.pubsub.broadcasts(broadcasting)
      broadcasts.collect { |b| JSON.parse(b) }.join("\n\n")
    end
end

**Deep Dive into the Bot Message Endpoint: A Meticulous Examination**

Alright, let's break this down. First, the file upload mechanism using `<input type="file">` looks clean and accessible. We're directly wrapping the file field within a label, which is excellent for screen readers. The "Name the bot" and "Save changes" button are equally well-structured. The "Delete this chat bot" button utilizes a `turbo_confirm` attribute for confirmation, which is the standard pattern we've established.

Now, the real meat: the HTTP API for bot messages. Let's get into the details:

1.  **Routing:** The route `POST /rooms/:room_id/:bot_key/messages` needs to be meticulously checked against the existing `/rooms` routes to avoid collisions. The constraint on `bot_key`, `bot_code`, using a regex like `/[^\/]+/` is crucial to handle potential edge cases with dots in the bot code, preventing routing errors.

2.  **Controller Concerns:** We need to carefully consider the concerns injected into our bot messages controller. We absolutely need `skip_forgery_protection` and `allow_unauthenticated_access` for this API to function. We may also need to skip `AllowBrowser` unless it is made to inherit properly to avoid any issues with `curl`, or shell scripts that may not send a `User-Agent`. Including `ActiveStorage::SetCurrent` ensures that attachment URLs in broadcasted messages resolve correctly (and the same as human authored messages!)!

3.  **Content Type & Encoding:** The `curl` command sends a `application/x-www-form-urlencoded` request. So, in the controller, it is essential to read the raw request body using `request.raw_post` (or `request.body.read`), and we need to be aware of the default `Content-Type` and its encoding, especially UTF-8! We must force the body to UTF-8 using `.force_encoding(Encoding::UTF_8)` to avoid encoding errors and prevent invalid HTML from rendering in Action Text! This prevents a lot of heartache later.

4.  **Error Handling**: The response codes are perfect; `201 Created` for success, and `422 Unprocessable Content`, `404 Not Found`, and `401 Unauthorized` for errors.

This analysis ensures that the bot messaging endpoint is both robust and secure.

**Analyzing Message Validation and Bot Interactions**

Okay, here's what's running through my head. I'm deep diving into the `Message` validation logic, specifically how it handles content. I see this `ensure_has_content` validation and immediately have a hunch, a potentially tricky interaction with rich text messages. What if a message has, say, an `OpengraphEmbed` or an `Attachment` *within* the rich text body? If `body.to_plain_text` is empty, or `body.blank?` is true, but the rich text container holds an OpenGraph embed or image inside, is the message *really* blank? Time to verify how Rails' `ActionText::RichText#blank?` works. Aha! It's actually `body.blank?`, which delegates to `ActionText::Content#blank?`, which, smartly, checks if `to_plain_text.blank? && empty_attachables?` - so embeds and images *aren't* considered blank! This is key.

Then I'm thinking about how `Message` uses that validation:

validate :ensure_has_content

The validation *expects* a body or an attachment. I realize that when `create!` or `create_with_attachment!` fails, Rails defaults to rescuing `ActiveRecord::RecordInvalid` and returning `422 Unprocessable Content`.

So, the next thought is: does this change anything? Let's check. Does any of the existing 297 tests in the suite break if we have this `validate :ensure_has_content`? A full test suite run is in order.

Aha! Next thought: What about a bot sending a message? Bots are allowed to send messages (using simple `curl` commands), but can a bot send an attachment? Let's check the prompt!

Okay, a bot can post a message with a simple `curl` command. The raw request body *becomes* the message body. Interesting. So, if we look at the happy/sad paths:
*   `201 Created` with `Location: /messages/:message_id` for valid messages.
*   `422 Unprocessable Content` if the body is empty and there's no attachment.
*   `404 Not Found` for bad room id.
*   `401 Unauthorized` for invalid bot code.

Here's the interesting part:  if `attachment_param` is an uploaded file (`params[:attachment].is_a?(ActionDispatch::Http::UploadedFile)` and `request.content_mime_type&.symbol == :multipart_form`): create the message with that attachment. Otherwise (no attachment, raw body) we read the raw request body!

And then I'm thinking about *how* to cleanly read that raw request body in *all* cases.  I need to ensure I can handle `curl -d "..."`, `--data-binary`, `text/plain` requests, integration tests (`post url, params: "Deploy...", headers: ...`), and using `post url, env: { "RAW_POST_DATA" => ... }`. The crucial question is how `request.raw_post` and `request.body.read` interact in Rails controllers *and* in `ActionDispatch::IntegrationTest`.

Right, let's test it out in a `RAILS_ENV=test bin/rails runner` session, and see what we get for these scenarios:
1.  `curl -d "Deploy of v1.2.3 finished ✅"` (`Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded`)
2.  `Content-Type: text/plain`
3.  No `Content-Type`
4.  Empty body `""`
5.  Body with `&` and `=` like `"a=1&b=2"` (and `application/x-www-form-urlencoded`
    content-type)!

Time to fire up that runner and get some answers.

**Eureka! A Clean, Elegant Fix to a Nasty Rails Problem**

Okay, stop everything, this is brilliant! I've just stumbled upon a real gem of a solution. Look at this stack trace! `ActionController::Instrumentation#process_action` calls `request.filtered_parameters` before the controller action even starts, which, in turn, calls `request.POST`. And that's where the problem lies. With the default `curl -d` using `application/x-www-form-urlencoded`, any unescaped percent signs in the message body, like "CPU at 95% warning," throw a `BadRequest` error due to invalid URL-encoding. And it gets worse! Malformed JSON, such as a request with `Content-Type: application/json` but a malformed body, also triggers a parse error from `ActionDispatch::Request#POST`. This is an unexpected behavior based on the prompt's instructions: bots are expected to send raw request bodies, without needing to include a `json` envelope.

But wait, I think I've cracked it. A 5-line Rails solution, that's all it takes! The key is within `Bots::MessagesController.dispatch(name, req, res)` (or an override on `process_action` or a Rack middleware), or even a dispatch hook. The genius of Rails' routing is that `dispatch` is called *before* `process_action`, *before* instrumentation, and *before* `filtered_parameters` is touched!

Here's the magic. Look at this line in the stack trace, `req.set_header("action_dispatch.request.request_parameters", {})`! Unless the content type is `multipart_form`, if we set `req.set_header("action_dispatch.request.request_parameters", {})` inside `Bots::MessagesController.dispatch(name, req, res)` then the magic happens!

1.  `req.raw_post` *still* reads the raw bytes from `req.env["rack.input"]`.
2.  `req.POST` returns an empty hash `{}`! No URL-decoding or JSON parsing is triggered!
3.  `req.filtered_parameters` only sees the `path_parameters` and `query_parameters`.

And the benefits? A whole bunch, actually:

*   `curl -d "CPU at 95% warning"` works perfectly.
*   `curl -H "Content-Type: application/json" -d "not json"` works just fine too.
*   The raw message body *isn't* logged in Rails parameter logs.
*   `params[:room_id]` and `params[:bot_code]` work as expected inside `Bots::MessagesController`.

I need to test this in `RAILS_ENV=test bin/rails runner` immediately, just to be absolutely sure. This could be a game-changer!

module User::Bot
  extend ActiveSupport::Concern

  included do
    belongs_to :creator, class_name: "User", optional: true
    has_many :bots, -> { bot }, class_name: "User", foreign_key: :creator_id, dependent: :nullify, inverse_of: :creator

    before_create :generate_bot_token, if: :bot?

    scope :without_bots, -> { not_bot }
    scope :active_bots, -> { active.bot }

    validates :name, presence: true, if: :bot?
  end

  class_methods do
    def create_bot!(attributes)
      bot.create!(**attributes.to_h.symbolize_keys, creator: Current.user)
    end

    def authenticate_bot(bot_key)
      bot_id, bot_token = bot_key.to_s.split("-", 2)
      return nil unless bot_id&.match?(/\A\d+\z/) && bot_token.present?

      if bot = active_bots.find_by(id: bot_id)
        bot if bot.bot_key.present? && ActiveSupport::SecurityUtils.secure_compare(bot.bot_key, bot_key.to_s)
      end
    end
  end

  def bot_key
    "#{id}-#{bot_token}" if bot? && bot_token.present?
  end

  private
    def generate_bot_token
      self.bot_token ||= self.class.generate_unique_secure_token
    end
end
EOF

  end

  test "returns 401 Unauthorized for invalid bot code or deleted bot" do

    assert_response :unauthorized

    post room_bot_messages_url(999999, "invalid.code"),
      params: "Hello",

      params: "Hello after delete",

    assert_response :unauthorized
  end

    assert_difference -> { @open_room.messages.count }, +1 do
      post room_bot_messages_url(@open_room, @bot.bot_key),
        params: { attachment: fixture_file_upload("moon.jpg", "image/jpeg") }
    end

    assert_response :created
    message = Message.last
    assert message.attachment?
    assert_equal "/messages/#{message.id}", response.headers["Location"]
  end
end

# This is in lib so we can use it in a thread pool without the Rails executor
class WebPush::Pool
  attr_reader :delivery_pool, :invalidation_pool, :connection, :invalid_subscription_handler

  def initialize(invalid_subscription_handler:)
    @delivery_pool = Concurrent::ThreadPoolExecutor.new(max_threads: 50, queue_size: 10000)
    @invalidation_pool = Concurrent::FixedThreadPool.new(1)
    @connection = Net::HTTP::Persistent.new(name: "web_push", pool_size: 150)
    @invalid_subscription_handler = invalid_subscription_handler
  end

  def queue(payload, subscriptions)
    subscriptions.find_each do |subscription|
      deliver_later(payload, subscription)
    end
  end

  def shutdown
    connection.shutdown
    shutdown_pool(delivery_pool)
    shutdown_pool(invalidation_pool)
  end

  private
    def deliver_later(payload, subscription)
      # Ensure any AR operations happen before we post to the thread pool
      notification = subscription.notification(**payload)
      subscription_id = subscription.id

      delivery_pool.post do
        deliver(notification, subscription_id)
      rescue Exception => e
        Rails.logger.error "Error in WebPush::Pool.deliver: #{e.class} #{e.message}"
      end
    rescue Concurrent::RejectedExecutionError
    end

    def deliver(notification, id)
      notification.deliver(connection: connection)
    rescue WebPush::ExpiredSubscription, OpenSSL::OpenSSLError => ex
      invalidate_subscription_later(id) if invalid_subscription_handler
    end

    def invalidate_subscription_later(id)
      invalidation_pool.post do
        invalid_subscription_handler.call(id)
      rescue Exception => e
        Rails.logger.error "Error in WebPush::Pool.invalid_subscription_handler: #{e.class} #{e.message}"

**A Successful Bot Integration - Now to Document and Solidify!**

Wow, that was exhilarating! Just look at that output! Real headless Chromium, Puma, ActionCable, and even `curl` are all working together seamlessly.

I'm incredibly pleased to see this end-to-end smoke test pass flawlessly. From signing in as a regular member to verifying the real-time ActionCable broadcast of the 'Deploy Bot', it all went exactly as planned. We created the bot, sent messages via `curl`, deleted it, and verified the correct HTTP status codes throughout. Even the native browser confirm() dialog worked perfectly.

This is a fantastic foundation. Now, it’s imperative that I take some time to capture all of these design insights. I'm going to start documenting everything in `docs/bots.md`. I want future extensions, and there will be many, to have a clear understanding of the whole system's context. I can't wait to write about bot file uploads, message editing and deletion with `Location: /messages/:message_id`, and even start thinking about webhook triggers and outbound bots. I’m thinking about bot token rotation too.

Once I've documented all of this, I need to make sure everything is in tip-top shape. I'll run all the standard checks: `bin/rails test`, `bin/rubocop`, `bundle exec brakeman`, and `env RAILS_ENV=test bin/rails db:seed:replant`, and of course, check the `git status` and `git diff` for a clean slate. With a solid set of tests, and a clearly documented design, we'll be ready for future bot functionality.

arguments.command:
cat <<'EOF' > docs/bots.md ## Chat Bots Architecture & Design Notes ### Data Model Bots are modeled as `User` records (`role: :bot`, see `app/models/user/bot.rb` and `app/models/user/role.rb`): - **`users.role`**: `enum :role, %i[ member administrator bot ]` (`2` = `bot`). - **`users.bot_token`**: 24-character base58 random credential generated via `generate_unique_secure_token` on creation (`nil` for human users and cleared to `nil` when a bot is deactivated). - **`users.creator_id`**: nullable self-referential foreign key (`on_delete: :nullify`) tracking which chat member created the bot. - **`users.password_digest`**: nullable so bots cannot authenticate via password/session login. Modeling bots on `User` means bots reuse existing `Membership`, `Room`, `Message` (`creator_id` FK to `users`), `User::Avatar`, `Message::Broadcasts`, and `Room::MessagePusher` pipelines without polymorphism or schema duplication: - **Open rooms**: `User#grant_membership_to_open_rooms` (`after_create_commit`) and `Rooms::Open#grant_access_to_all_users` include active bots automatically. - **Closed & direct rooms**: `Rooms::ClosedsController`, `Rooms::DirectsController`, and `Autocompletable::UsersController` query `User.active`, allowing bots to be added to rooms the same way as people. - **Human-only surfaces**: `User.without_bots` excludes bots from the `/account/edit` member management list, session login/transfer, IP bans, and direct-message sidebar placeholders. - **Soft deletion**: Deleting a bot calls `User#deactivate`, setting `status: :deactivated`, clearing `bot_token: nil`, and removing non-direct room memberships while keeping historical messages authored by the bot intact. ### Ownership & Authorization - Any signed-in member can access `/bots`, `/bots/new`, and `POST /bots`. - `/bots` (`BotsController#index`) lists `Current.user.bots.active` for regular members and `User.active_bots` for administrators on a single page without pagination, with `Cache-Control: no-store` and `turbo-cache-control: no-store`. - `User::Role#can_administer?(record)` returns `false` for bots themselves, `true` for administrators, and `true` when `self == record&.creator`, authorizing `edit`, `update`, and `destroy` on `BotsController`. ### Bot Code & HTTP Messaging API - **Bot code format**: `"#{id}-#{bot_token}"` (`User#bot_key`). `User.authenticate_bot` verifies numeric `id`, active bot status, and compares the full `bot_key` via `ActiveSupport::SecurityUtils.secure_compare`. - **Log hygiene**: `:bot_code` (alongside `:token` and `:_key`) is filtered in `config/initializers/filter_parameter_logging.rb`. - **Endpoint**: `POST /rooms/:room_id/:bot_code/messages` (`Bots::MessagesController#create`). - Inherits from `ActionController::Base` (including `ActiveStorage::SetCurrent`, `BlockBannedRequests`, `SetCurrentRequest`, `VersionHeaders`) so CLI User-Agents are never blocked by browser version gates. - Overrides `self.dispatch` for non-multipart requests to set `action_dispatch.request.request_parameters = {}` so raw shell payloads sent via `curl -d "..."` (`application/x-www-form-urlencoded`) containing `%`, `&`, or arbitrary bytes never trigger `ActionController::BadRequest` before reaching the action, and raw message text is kept out of parameter logs. - Reads `request.raw_post` as UTF-8, HTML-escapes text, converts newlines to `
`, and creates the message via `@room.messages.create_with_attachment!`. - Responds `401 Unauthorized` (invalid/revoked bot code, checked before room lookup to avoid room ID enumeration), `404 Not Found` (unknown room or bot not a member of the room), `422 Unprocessable Content` (blank body and no attachment, enforced by `Message#ensure_has_content`), or `201 Created` with `Location: /messages/:message_id`. ### Notes for Future Extensions - **`Location: /messages/:message_id`**: Returning `/messages/:message_id` provides a canonical message identifier that future bot endpoints (e.g., bot message updates, deletions, or file/attachment endpoints) can target while verifying `message.creator == authenticated_bot`. - **Attachments**: `Message#ensure_has_content` and `Bots::MessagesController#message_params` already coordinate with `Message::Attachment` (`create_with_attachment!`), making dedicated multipart or binary file-upload extensions straightforward. EOF bin/rails test && bin/rubocop && bundle exec brakeman --quiet --no-pager --exit-on-warn --exit-on-error && env RAILS_ENV=test bin/rails db:seed:replant && git status

  - New bots automatically join all open rooms and can be added to closed and direct rooms alongside people, while `User.without_bots` keeps human-only surfaces (account member list, session sign-in/transfer, IP bans, and direct-message sidebar placeholders) scoped to human users.
  - Deleting a bot deactivates it and clears its `bot_token`, revoking its ability to post messages while preserving historical messages it authored.
- **Bot management UI (`BotsController`, `app/views/bots/*`, `app/views/accounts/edit.html.erb`)**:

- **Bot HTTP messaging API (`Bots::MessagesController`, `POST /rooms/:room_id/:bot_code/messages`)**:
  - Accepts the raw request body directly as the message body, authenticates the bot, verifies room membership, broadcasts to connected clients, and enqueues Web Push notifications with the bot as author.
  - Responds with `201 Created` (`Location: /messages/:message_id`), `422 Unprocessable Content` (empty body and no attachment), `404 Not Found` (invalid/inaccessible room), and `401 Unauthorized` (invalid or deleted bot code).
